newsitem.title: GERMANY: BoE's George - EMU candidates must be aware of risks.
newsitem.headline: BoE's George - EMU candidates must be aware of risks.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George said that even those states that do meet the Maastricht convergence criteria should should think hard about the risk of entering European monetary union (EMU) if they have to do so with considerable structural divergence.

"The full and lasting convergence of national economies is necessary before the irrevocable fixing of nominal exchange rates can be envisaged," George said in a guest commentary published in Germany's Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on Tuesday. The commentary was published in German.

"We do not know yet how many countries will fulfil the criteria in 1998," George said. "But even those that do should think long and hard about the risks of joining EMU if they have to do so with considerable structural divergence."
George said the "mythology of exchange rate management" was such that many were convinced they would suffer under uncertain exchange rates or would suffer in the foreseeable future, George said.
"Such fears seem to be misplaced," George said. "Exchange rate movements are doubtless a bother for exporters and importers. Currency exchange and hedging trades cost money.

"Nevertheless the damage is limited compared with the potential for real macroeconomic disruption that can arise if exchange rate relations are excessively strained in defiance of economic realities."
George also said he did not believe the economy of a country had much to fear from devaluations to gain competitive advantages, certainly not by other EU members.
As long as countries that that did not take part in the first wave of EMU pursued a responsible economic policy the probablity of nominal exchange rate swings would decline, George said.
And if a country did not succeed in pushing through discipline any devaluation to gain a competitive advantage would be offset by higher domestic costs, George said.
"In short - our vital national interests and our common interest as a European Union are based on the pursuit of healthy domestic policies," George said.

"In the measure in which economies converge we will experience how real and nominal exchange rates stabilise. Unter such circumstances we can contemplate a formal coupling of the exchange rates with more confidence. In that case the cart would be where it belongs - behind the horse."
